title: Latency fingerprinting & 'hoverbench' probe notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick lab-notes for a new micro-probing harness ("hoverbench") and a set of fingerprinting experiments to isolate tail-causing interactions between continuous batching, timeouts, and kernel hotpaths. The goal is narrow: find reproducible conditions that produce >2x 99.9p relative to median and identify mitigations that are low-risk to roll into the scheduler.

Summary of hypothesis and approach:
- Hypothesis: intermittent kernel hitch on the quantized attention path (int8 GEMM + fused postprocess kernels) amplifies when batch formation mixes 3 request-length cohorts and the flush timeout lines up with slower memcpy/stream scheduling on the GPU.
- Approach: produce synthetic microtraces with controlled arrival jitter and request-length distributions; sweep batch_size cap (8/16/32), timeout ms (2/5/10/20), and fairness weights (age-decay 0/0.5/0.9). Capture full microtraces (enqueue timestamp, batch start, kernel timeline, stream syncs) and lightweight perf counters.

What "hoverbench" does (notes to self):
- Generates Poisson or bursty arrivals configurable via CV of interarrival times.
- Tag requests with length cohorts: short (8 tokens), medium (64), long (512).
- Can pin affinities so certain cohorts prefer slot X to emulate KV-cache locality effects.
- Emits CSV microtrace suitable for our tracer ingestion and sidecar visualizer.
- Adds optional gpu-stream-stagger flag to jitter host->device memcpy start time (0..5ms) to test overlap sensitivity.

Key experiment runs (high level):
1) Baseline: batch_cap=32 timeout=10ms fairness=0.5 arrival=CVMix (0.4/0.4/0.2 short/med/long) => 99p=45ms 99.9p=210ms (unstable, wide spikes)
2) Tight timeout: batch_cap=16 timeout=2ms fairness=0.9 => 99.9p down to 120ms, but median increases slightly (extra small batches)
3) Jittered memcpy (gpu-stream-stagger=2ms) with baseline params => 99.9p reduced by ~22% (210ms -> 165ms).
4) Pin long-cohort affinity to separate slot (prefer dedicated worker) => 99.9p reduced by ~35% and tail spikes become rarer.

Observed root signals (profiling evidence):
- Repro traces show a recurring pattern: small batch formed (2-4 short requests) executes quickly, then a long request arrives and is coalesced causing kernel that uses a different quantized path to be launched on a pinned stream. If the previous stream hasn't completed host->device copies due to DMA scheduling, the long kernel waits on stream synchronization and then executes with extra serial memcpy operations. This gap correlates with 99.9p spikes.
- nvprof/NSys snapshots show bursts of cudaMemcpyAsync being serialized on the same stream when host code staggers copies. On machines with older driver stacks this effect is exaggerated.
- CPU-side traces show scheduler flush call happens at timeout boundary which often aligns with host thread building the batch and doing synchronous buffer prep; the variance in that preparation amplifies tail.

Immediate low-risk mitigations to try (ranked):
- Staggered flush jitter: randomize flush time inside [0..timeout_ms/2] to avoid synchronized flushes across lanes (low code risk).
- Small-slot prefill: require minimal prefill of 1-2 tokens from long cohort before coalescing with many shorts (heuristic, needs A/B).
- Overlap memcpy: ensure buffer uploads use separate pinned staging buffers and schedule cudaMemcpyAsync on a dedicated transfer stream to allow better overlap. (Medium risk; driver/allocator interactions).
- Affinity soft-separation: prefer placing long-cohort requests to reserved slots to avoid mixed-kernel launches (operational complexity).

Metrics to capture for each run (must collect):
- per-request: enqueue_ts, batch_start_ts, dispatch_ts, first_byte_ts, completion_ts, cohort_label, slot_id
- per-batch: batch_size, timeout_triggered(bool), kernel_variant_id, stream_id, bytes_uploaded
- system: NVidia driver version, kernel-version, cpu cores, numa, GPU model, host DMA stats

Open questions / TODOs:
- Is the quantized kernel itself non-preemptible and causing serialized memcpy on certain driver/architecture combos? Need kernel dev input (cc: @Miguel).
- Can caching small pre-allocated pinned buffers for uploads reduce variance more than stream staggering? Quick microbenchmark.
- Should we expose the jittered-flush knob as an opt-in per-tenant policy vs global default? Safety and fairness implications.
- Run full sweep on A100 vs H100 vs 3090 in cloud; early results show H100 less sensitive but still exhibits tail under mixed cohorts.

Commands / repro snippets (hoverbench):
- ./hoverbench --arrival=cvmix --mix=0.5,0.35,0.15 --batch_cap=32 --timeout_ms=10 --gpu-stagger=0 --run-id=hb01 > hb01.csv
- python tools/trace_ingest.py --input hb01.csv --out hb01.trace
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt --output nsys-hb01 ./serving-runtime --replay hb01.trace

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc intentionally mixes quick heuristics with trace evidence; it's a working artifact. I'm logging here so we don't duplicate probing effort.
- Priority next steps: (1) implement jittered flush and run a 48-hr synthetic flood, (2) try transfer-stream prototype on one canary node, (3) open kernel-level investigation ticket if reproducible on H100.

Unresolved: are we measuring the right fairness metric? Current age-decay parameter reduces tail in synthetic tests but may penalize small interactive workloads in production — need production trace replay to validate tradeoffs.

Signed-off: Aisha (notes), will sync with Jordan/Miguel/PRiya in next sync.
